source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (experience-following)
finding: Agents copy retrieved cases. The closer the new task is to a stored case, the closer the output is to that case's output. The input-output similarity correlation approaches Pearson r of 1 once memory grows.
numbers: Four agents (RegAgent, EHRAgent, AgentDriver, CIC-IoT). Fixed-memory runs showed lower input and output similarity than add-all runs.
limits: Correlation shown in figures. The agent set is small and partly synthetic (RegAgent).
agent_relevance: Retrieved cases act almost as a template. So the retain step decides what the agent will later copy. A quality gate on retain is a control point, not a detail.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (retain: add-all vs selective)
finding: Retain step: adding every run to memory is worse than a strict filter, and sometimes worse than adding nothing.
numbers: Score for RegAgent / EHRAgent / AgentDriver / CIC-IoT. Add-all 55.48 / 13.05 / 32.32 / 59.90. Coarse LLM judge C1 63.18 / 26.19 / 36.92 / 74.00. C3 (judge fine-tuned on 300 trajectories) 67.35 / 34.66 / 47.37 / 79.50. Strict (human-oracle) 70.95 / 38.50 / 51.00 / 85.40.
limits: The strict evaluator is an oracle comparing to ground truth; not available in real use.
agent_relevance: Retain only on verified success (code check or held-out check). Never retain on the model's own judgement. Matches G2 and G3.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (error propagation)
finding: Errors in stored cases spread to later tasks. Add-all and coarse-judge runs open a growing gap to an error-free memory (same retrievals, ground-truth outputs).
numbers: With a strict evaluator on AgentDriver the gap closed and passed the error-free variant after about 2000 executions.
limits: Only two agents shown (RegAgent, AgentDriver).
agent_relevance: Store an outcome flag with each case and let later results re-score it. One bad case can poison its neighbours.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (deletion, misaligned replay)
finding: Deleting cases with low downstream utility (history-based deletion) helped when the utility judge was reliable. With a noisy judge it hurt. Periodic deletion cut memory with small loss.
numbers: Strict evaluator, no deletion vs history-based: AgentDriver 85.40 vs 89.60 (memory 904 vs 788); EHRAgent 38.67 vs 42.06 (1012 vs 784). RegAgent combined deletion: memory 2938 to 890, score 70.95 to 66.58. Coarse C1 history-based on CIC-IoT: 74.00 to 68.80.
limits: Gain depends on judge quality; the same method helped one agent and hurt another with a GPT-4o-mini judge. Under task shift, periodic deletion was the more stable.
agent_relevance: Add a forget step driven by later outcomes of the case, only where the outcome signal is code-checked. Otherwise use plain size-bounded forgetting.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (frozen memory baseline)
finding: A frozen memory with no additions still beat noisy-judge additions on several agents. More memory is not always better.
numbers: On RegAgent, AgentDriver and CIC-IoT a fixed memory sometimes beat coarse-judge runs. Fine-tuning the judge on only 300 trajectories (C3) was enough to beat add-all and the other coarse judges.
limits: The frozen-memory table row was not readable in the extracted text; the claim rests on the paper's prose.
agent_relevance: A small frozen verified case base is a strong baseline. Beat it before adding online retain.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) Remembering to Forget: competence-preserving case deletion
finding: Classic retain-side result. Random and utility-based deletion cut the competence of a case base. Footprint deletion (keep pivotal and support cases) held it.
numbers: Property-valuation CBR, 50 cases, 160 targets, benchmark competence 100%. After the swamping limit, random deletion ended at 86% and utility deletion at 80%; footprint and footprint-utility stayed at 100%. At a limit just over 25 cases, footprint policies reached about 90% of benchmark vs about 60% for random and utility. Case base: 20 pivotal, 5 auxiliary, 25 support (7 groups), 0 spanning.
quote: Surprisingly, random deletion can work very well
limits: One toy domain, nearest-neighbour retrieval, simulated. No human or LLM study.
agent_relevance: If the agent's case store must stay small, delete by coverage (cases no other case can stand in for), not by how often a case was used.

source: Smyth and Keane (1995) (utility problem boundary)
finding: Retain has a cost: a bigger case base makes retrieval slower (the swamping problem). Deleting to fix speed can lose competence.
numbers: Competence began to fall almost at once after the swamping limit was reached (25 trials) and ended at 80% (utility) and 86% (random).
limits: Simulated trials on one data set.
agent_relevance: Plan a size cap and a coverage-based delete from the start.

source: Pan, Yang, Pan and Li (2005) Competence Driven Case-Base Mining (AAAI-05)
finding: Follow-up that tests Smyth and Keane's footprint deletion with noise. The footprint policy keeps outlier and noisy cases as pivotal, so it is sensitive to noise. A kernel-based mining method kept competence higher at small sizes.
numbers: Spiral and UCI data sets, 1-NN accuracy. Their method rose fastest as case-base size went from 1% to 5% of the data; at 25% size the gap to case deletion was very small. Noise-ratio curves are in a figure only.
limits: Classification data sets, not agent tasks. No exact noise numbers in text.
agent_relevance: Coverage-based keeping fails when the store holds wrong cases: a rare wrong case looks irreplaceable. Gate by correctness first, coverage second.

source: Lopez de Mantaras et al. (2005) Retrieval, reuse, revision and retention in case-based reasoning (Knowledge Engineering Review 20)
finding: Field review of the 4R cycle by 13 co-authors. It covers cognitive foundations, the link to analogical reasoning, and research on each R.
numbers: Pages 215-240, vol 20 no 3. Only the abstract page was read; no per-R findings were opened.
limits: Full text not opened. No per-R effect sizes from this source.
agent_relevance: Use as the map; take effect sizes from the empirical papers.

source: Re4: Optimizing CBR system for functional test script generation with LLMs (KDD 2025)
finding: Full 4R system with a 7B LLM. Plain CBR (three similar cases in the prompt) beats SFT alone by a wide margin. Tuning retrieve and reuse adds a smaller gain.
numbers: Function F1 (DCN / SP): Naive SFT 49.46 / 38.71; Naive CBR 64.01 / 54.60; CBR 64.67 / 55.83; CBR+SFT 67.87 / 57.98; CBR+Re4 70.11 / 61.92. Test sets 689 and 366. Retriever finetuning ablation about 1 point FF1. No finetuning: 66.06 / 59.17.
limits: One run per method, no variance. Two units of one company, noisy data. Revise is done by human engineers and not ablated. Only function correctness measured.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain comes from putting retrieved cases in the prompt (about +15 F1 over SFT), not from tuning. A cheap retrieve step is the main lever.

source: Re4 (retain, online evaluation)
finding: Retain matters online: a growing case bank beat a frozen case bank (RAG-like).
numbers: About 6,000 recent samples across two units. CBR+Re4 over CBR+SFT: +2.75% (DCN) and +10.08% (SP) FF1. Without Retain it significantly underperforms; exact values in a figure only.
limits: Retain was not tested offline. The paper does not say if gains are relative or absolute. Human engineers revise the stored scripts, so stored cases are verified.
agent_relevance: Retain helps when stored cases are verified by an outside party. Fits Xiong et al.

source: Guo et al. (2024) DS-Agent: automated data science with CBR
finding: CBR agent for data-science tasks. Retrieved solutions cut cost and raise one-pass success. One retrieved case worked best.
numbers: 30 tasks (12 development, 18 deployment). Development success GPT-4 100%. Deployment one-pass: GPT-3.5 85% vs best baseline 56% (GPT-3.5) and 60% (GPT-4); Mixtral 6% to 31%. Average best rank GPT-4: full 2.08, without ReviseRank 2.58, without CBR 3.41. Cost per run GPT-4 $1.60 development vs $0.135 deployment.
limits: Small task set; some data sets after 2021. Retain not ablated. More than one example case hurt in deployment.
agent_relevance: Reuse of one close past solution beats several. Retrieval beat a random one-shot example. Revision by ranking added value (+0.5 rank).

source: DS-Agent (retrieval number boundary)
finding: Zero examples was worst, but performance dropped quickly as more cases were added; one case was best.
numbers: Mean rank in deployment (lower is better), GPT-4: zero-shot 28.2, one-shot 28.0, DS-Agent 12.7; GPT-3.5: 30.8 / 35.0 / 17.1; Mixtral 45.3 / 39.4 / 35.5. Cost cut 92.5% (GPT-3.5) and 91.5% (GPT-4).
limits: Case-count curves are in figures only. The paper text conflicts with its table on rank direction.
agent_relevance: Matches Memento on small K.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: CBR for retrieval augmented generation in legal QA
finding: Weak result: case retrieval added little over no retrieval, because the model already knew the domain.
numbers: Casebase 2,084 cases, 32 test cases. Cosine similarity of answer to reference: no-RAG 0.8967; best (hybrid AnglEBERT, k=3, full case) 0.9141, about 1.94% relative. LegalBERT k=3 0.9045. Significant at 95% vs no-RAG.
limits: Tiny synthetic test set; answers scored only by embedding cosine; LLM-made data. Several cases were hard to combine in one prompt.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: when the model already holds the knowledge, retrieved cases add little. Test against a no-retrieval arm first.

source: Memento: fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs (2025)
finding: Case bank with a planner that retrieves past cases and an executor. Removing case-based reasoning lowers every score. Gains peak at about four cases.
numbers: DeepResearcher F1/PM: without CBR 59.9/72.2 vs Memento 66.6/80.4. SimpleQA 81.0/89.7 vs 84.7/95.0. HLE 22.2/17.4 vs 26.7/24.4. Retrieved cases K: 0 -> 59.9 F1, 1 -> 63.6, 4 -> 64.5 (best), 8 -> 64.1, 32 -> 63.9. GAIA validation 87.88, test 79.40. Iteration 5: parametric 85.44, non-parametric 84.85, none 84.47.
limits: Judge is GPT-4o-mini; no variance; contamination suspected on DeepResearcher; GAIA ranking text conflicts with its table.
agent_relevance: Same as DS-Agent: a few cases (1-4) help, many do not. Non-parametric memory gives most of the learned memory's gain (about 0.6 point gap at iteration 5).

source: Memento (cost and planner boundary)
finding: The case bank saturates and cost climbs with difficulty. A slow deliberate planner did worse than a fast one.
numbers: GAIA validation: deliberative planner 63.03 vs fast 70.91 average. Tokens per task about 26k (Level 1), 48k (Level 2), 121k (Level 3).
limits: No variance; small judge model.
agent_relevance: Cap retrieved cases at about four. Count the cost of the retrieve step.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: The agent stores trajectories (retain), retrieves them (retrieve), and distils text insights (revise the rules). Both parts help, in different tasks.
numbers: gpt-3.5 success: HotpotQA ReAct 28.0, ExpeL 39.0, insights-only 36, retrieve-only 31. ALFWorld ReAct 40.0, ExpeL 59.0, insights-only 50, retrieve-only 55, random trajectories 42.5, reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5. WebShop score ReAct 0.665 vs ExpeL 0.701. Transfer HotpotQA to FEVER: ReAct 63, ExpeL 70.
limits: Closed API model, text only, four-fold validation. Few-shot examples alone did no better than ReAct.
agent_relevance: Similarity-based retrieval of trajectories beats random trajectories by 16.5 points on ALFWorld, so the similarity does real work. Insights matter more for reasoning tasks, trajectories for acting tasks.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank
finding: Distils strategies from both successes and failures. Adding failures helped ReasoningBank but hurt AWM.
numbers: WebArena success No Memory / Synapse / AWM / ReasoningBank: Gemini-2.5-flash 40.5 / 42.1 / 44.1 / 48.8; Gemini-2.5-pro 46.7 / 47.7 / 47.6 / 53.9; Claude-3.7-sonnet 41.7 / 42.6 / 40.8 / 46.3. SWE-Bench-Verified flash 34.2 to 38.8, pro 54.0 to 57.4. Failure ablation (Shopping): ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7; AWM 44.4 to 42.2; Synapse 40.6 to 41.7. Judge accuracy 72.7%.
limits: Mind2Web gains are small in absolute terms (cross-task 3.3 to 4.8). The limitations section was not read. Best-of-5 test-time scaling reached 55.1 from 49.7.
agent_relevance: Learning from failure pays only when memory is written as lessons, not raw trajectories. Raw failure cases can hurt (AWM -2.2).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Reusable workflows extracted from past runs raise web-agent success. Offline and online versions are similar in-domain. Online is better on unseen websites.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4) total success: BrowserGym 23.5, SteP (human workflows) 33.0, AWM online 35.5; steps 5.9. Mind2Web cross-task step SR: MindAct 36.2, AWM 45.1 (task SR 2.0 to 4.8). Cross-domain step SR: 18.6 to 32.6 (offline), 35.5 (online). Combining offline and online workflows gave no gain (44.5).
limits: Mind2Web task SR stays at 1-5%. Online cross-website SR 1.6 vs MindAct 2.0. Workflow actions were called in only 18.5% of tasks. Fixed workflows fail on changing pages.
agent_relevance: Abstracting cases into workflows beats raw cases. Rule-based vs LM-based induction was nearly equal (35.6 vs 35.5).

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet
finding: Memory curation with a model-written cheatsheet. Big gains on some tasks, none or harm on others, strongly tied to model strength.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet: AIME 2024 23.3 baseline, 36.7 with empty cheatsheet, 50.0 cumulative curation; AIME 2025 6.7 to 36.7. Full history appended: 26.7 and 6.7. GPT-4o Game of 24: 10 to 99. GPT-4o MMLU-Pro Engineering 53.2 to 44.0 (harm). GPT-4o-mini mostly flat. Majority vote on AIME 2024 stayed 23.33.
limits: Each AIME subset has 30 questions (1 question = 3.3 points). No variance reported. Part of the gain is from the structured prompt alone (empty-memory arm).
agent_relevance: Part of the memory gain is a prompt effect: compare with an empty-memory arm. Curated memory beat both raw history and plain retrieval on AIME. Retrieval can bring weak examples and hurt.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: The revise step fails when the model judges itself. Accuracy drops after self-correction and rises only when the true answer is given.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1). GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CommonSenseQA 89.7. GSM8K with 6 responses: debate 83.2 vs self-consistency 85.3.
limits: Three tasks, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only. Different prompts could shift the drop.
agent_relevance: Revise must be driven by real output (a test or checker), as in G2. Self-judged revise loses accuracy.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Revise from an external signal plus a written reflection helps on code and acting tasks. It fails where the signal is bad or the task needs exploration.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1. MBPP Python 77.1 vs 80.1 (worse); false-positive rate of self-written tests 16.3% vs 1.4% on HumanEval. HumanEval Rust ablation: base 0.60, no test generation 0.52, no reflection 0.60, full 0.68. HotPotQA: reflection adds 8 points over episodic memory alone. WebShop: no significant gain over ReAct.
limits: Self-written tests can be wrong; local minima; sliding-window memory.
agent_relevance: Revise needs a trustworthy checker. Where checks give false passes, revising can drop below baseline.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Case-based or rule-based: how do transformers do the math?
finding: Language models solve arithmetic mostly by case matching, not by rule. Held-out regions of the input space show holes.
numbers: Random split: 100% on all data sets. Leave-square-out (441-sample square held out): Llama-2-7B trained from scratch on base addition 30.2% vs 92% on random split. GPT-3.5 zero-shot base addition 8.8% +/- 10.5; similar examples helped more than random (p < 0.001). Rule-following fine-tuning: GPT-3.5 over 95% on 12-digit addition with 100 samples.
limits: Pretrained Llama-2-7B on base-9 addition showed no obvious holes, so the claim is uncertain for pretrained models. One narrow domain.
agent_relevance: Models retrieve near cases implicitly. Reuse beyond the cases seen is where they break, so add an explicit adaptation step for out-of-range inputs.

source: Liu et al. (2021) What makes good in-context examples for GPT-3? (KATE)
finding: Retrieve step in prompts: nearest-neighbour examples beat random examples.
numbers: IMDB accuracy random 87.95 +/- 2.74 vs KATE 91.99 (SST-2 tuned 93.43). ToTTo BLEU 28.4 vs 40.3. NQ exact match 28.6 vs 40.0 to 41.6. WQ 41.0 vs 47.7 to 50.6. TriviaQA 59.2 vs 57.5 (untuned encoder, below random) to 62.4.
limits: Only GPT-3; dev sets for ToTTo and TriviaQA; abstract headline numbers do not match tables. Plain kNN label voting about 50.2 on sentiment.
agent_relevance: The retrieval encoder matters, and an untuned one can be no better than random. Example order changed NQ EM only 41.6 vs 42.8.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the role of demonstrations
finding: Rival explanation for why retrieved cases help: format, label space and input distribution matter more than correct labels.
numbers: Random labels cost only 0-5% absolute (average 2.6% classification, 1.7% multi-choice) over 12 model setups and 26 data sets. Out-of-distribution inputs cost 3-16%. Random English words as labels cost 5-16% for direct models. GPT-J lost nearly 10% when all labels were wrong.
limits: Classification and multi-choice only. Later work found negated labels hurt. Averages hide a 14-point drop on one data set.
agent_relevance: Part of the retrieve-reuse gain is format and distribution cues, not the solution in the case. Test with a case whose solution is wrong.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Self-generated cases (the model recalls its own related problems) match or beat retrieved cases for large models, and lose for small ones.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot CoT 75.8, few-shot CoT 76.7, analogical 77.8; text-davinci-003 50.3 / 54.0 / 61.0. MATH GPT-3.5 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3. Generated vs retrieved on GSM8K: curie-001 2 vs 3, davinci-001 9 vs 11, davinci-002 48 vs 47, davinci-003 61 vs 57. Codeforces GPT-4 Acc@1 16 to 19 (50 problems).
limits: Codeforces set has only 50 problems. 12 of 50 errors came from exemplars that did not fit; 8 followed misleading exemplars.
agent_relevance: When no case base exists, the model may recall its own cases, but only a strong model. More output tokens.

source: Hatalis et al. (2025) Review of CBR for LLM agents
finding: Review that argues CBR gives LLM agents memory and explanation. It has no experiments of its own. Its table of CBR vs chain-of-thought vs RAG uses qualitative labels only.
numbers: Only exact figure is DS-Agent's 100% development success and 99% one-pass. Other cited results (CB-GDA, CBR-RAG, triage, code generation) have no numbers.
limits: Attribution muddled (Wiratunga 2024 cited for several works). No limits section. Its claim of clear advantages is untested here.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the review as evidence. Go to the primary papers.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Human retrieval follows surface similarity. Judged soundness follows shared relational structure. The two come apart.
numbers: Exp 1 quality-of-reminding rating: 2.36 for surface matches (shared objects plus first-order relations), 1.48 for true analogies, 0.86 for relations-only matches. Analogy had the top soundness rating (4.40 of 5).
limits: College students, written recall of old stories from new cues, delay about a week. Lab stories, not expert problems.
agent_relevance: The retrieve step will favour look-alike cases over same-structure cases. Embedding nearest-neighbour is not a measure of usefulness.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: Object-level overlap alone beat purely relational overlap in retrieval (Exp 3).
numbers: Recalled: surface plus first-order relation matches 52%, object-attribute-only matches 17%, purely relational analogies 7%.
limits: Cued recall, not spontaneous problem solving.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by distant structure needs extra help (index by problem type or abstract rule), not just a similarity search.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: The gap is not missing knowledge. At recognition people used the relational structure.
numbers: One week after study, forced choice: the literally similar match was chosen over the surface-only match 82% of the time.
limits: Recognition is easier than recall; shows encoding was adequate, not that retrieval is cheap.
agent_relevance: Storing a case with its structure is not enough. The retrieval cue must carry structure too.

source: Gentner, Rattermann, Forbus (1993) The roles of similarity in transfer: separating retrievability from inferential soundness
finding: MAC/FAC (cheap content-vector scan, then structure-sensitive match) reproduces the human retrievability order literal > surface > analogy >= mere appearance.
numbers: In simulation the first stage returned on average 3.3 memory items per probe; the second stage kept the structural best.
limits: Model fit by the same lab to its own data. Few independent tests.
agent_relevance: A two-stage retrieve (broad cheap scan, then structural filter done by code) is a tested design for the retrieve step.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Re-run of the Gick and Holyoak radiation-problem paradigm. Without a hint, reuse of a stored analogue stays near the 10% baseline unless the learner compared two analogues.
numbers: Exp 1: two analogues total 71% vs one analogue plus control story 41%. One-analogue no-comparison group 25% before hint to 30% after; comparison group 16% to 53%. Baseline with no analogue about 10%.
limits: Students, one session. Cell sizes small.
agent_relevance: Reuse needs an abstract schema; comparing two cases builds it. Supports comparing examples in S2 and a stored lesson in S9.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Delay shrinks reuse. Before the hint no condition beat the 10% baseline in the delay experiment.
numbers: Exp 2 total solutions with hint: 65% at 30-minute delay vs 42% at one week. Before-hint rates for comparison groups 11% (30 min) and 0% (1 week).
limits: A hint is a retrieval cue, which the agent only gets if code supplies it.
agent_relevance: Old cases need an explicit retrieval trigger. Do not wait for the model to remember.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Quality of the schema the learner wrote predicted transfer.
numbers: Appropriate vs inappropriate schemas: 40% vs 6% in one contrast (p<.02); 32% vs 12%; and 68% vs 39% when hint-aided.
limits: Correlational inside the experiment: schema quality was not randomised. n=7 to 20 per cell.
agent_relevance: At retain, store a short abstracted rule with the case and check it, not only the raw trace.

source: Kubricht, Lu, Holyoak (2015) Animation facilitates source understanding and spontaneous analogical transfer
finding: Richer, dynamic encoding of the source raised spontaneous reuse. A static diagram did not. Also restates the classic benchmark of about 10% unaided, about 30% with a dissimilar story, about 80% after a hint.
numbers: Spontaneous transfer 55% verbal, 50% verbal plus diagram, 81% verbal plus animation (42 per condition, 126 total; animation vs verbal chi-square 6.60, p=.01). Total after hint 83%, 69%, 90%.
quote: people often failed to spontaneously notice the relevance of a source analog
limits: One lab, one cannon-and-fortress source. The 1980/1983 originals were only seen second-hand here.
agent_relevance: How the stored case is encoded matters more than adding a picture. Store the mechanism.

source: Kubricht, Lu, Holyoak (2015) Animation facilitates source understanding and spontaneous analogical transfer
finding: Individual-difference moderator: animation helped low fluid-intelligence participants most (median split on a 12-item Raven).
numbers: 45 low-Raven and 57 high-Raven participants. The animation advantage in spontaneous transfer was largest for the low group and only marginal over diagram for the high group.
limits: Subgroup analysis from a single study with a short abridged Raven.
agent_relevance: Weaker reasoners (small models) gain most from rich case support. Test the scaffold per model size.

source: Aha, Kibler, Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms
finding: Retain-only-errors (IB2) saves storage and loses accuracy; a pass/fail record per case (IB3) fixes the noise problem and cuts storage further.
numbers: Accuracy / percent stored. Voting: IB1 91.8/100, IB2 90.9/11.1, IB3 91.6/7.4. LED display: 70.5, 62.4 (41.5%), 71.7 (28.7%). Hungarian heart: IB1 58.7, IB2 55.9, IB3 80.5 (7.5% stored), decision tree C4 78.2.
limits: Small UCI datasets from 1991, one-nearest-neighbour. IB3 degrades with many irrelevant attributes and with a 95% acceptance confidence.
agent_relevance: Keep a use-and-outcome record per stored case. Modern history-based deletion repeats this idea.

source: Aha, Kibler, Albert (1991) Instance-based learning algorithms
finding: Retaining only the cases the memory got wrong lets noise in: a noisy case is always misclassified, so it is always stored.
numbers: At 10% training noise, 20 of IB2's 76 saved instances (26.3%) were noisy; average 28.3% of saved instances noisy at that level. 50 trials.
limits: Artificial domain.
agent_relevance: If retain keys on the agent's own errors, bad labels flow in. Retain only cases confirmed by a code check.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory
finding: Gains from experience reuse depend on how similar the tasks in the stream are to each other. Plain task-level retrieval stays competitive with elaborate memory modules. Storing failures hurt baselines.
numbers: Pearson r between gain over a history baseline and within-dataset task similarity: 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Big gains on PDDL and ALFWorld, small on AIME-25 and GPQA. ALFWorld steps 22.6 to 11.5.
limits: Ten datasets, two backbones for the correlation. The results tables were garbled in the PDF text, so only text claims are recorded.
agent_relevance: Turn memory on only for problem classes that recur (S0 gate). Test any memory design against plain ExpRAG-style retrieval at equal tokens.

source: Sarukkai et al. (2025) Self-generated in-context examples improve LLM agents for sequential decision-making tasks
finding: Plain accumulation of the agent's own successful runs, retrieved by cosine similarity, gave large gains. Curation added more. Gains showed diminishing returns and unstable additions.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini: ALFWorld 73% to 89%, Wordcraft 55% to 64%, InterCode-SQL 75% to 79%; 93% on ALFWorld with curation. The first 25% of added tasks gave most of the gain. Best-utility exemplars beat worst-utility exemplars at equal database size.
limits: Five trials with wide trial-to-trial spread; some added trajectories lowered performance within a run.
agent_relevance: Self-made cases work when success is checkable. Cap memory, and track retrieval-weighted outcomes per case.
